record.summary: Computed Vmin(p) (least v in 4Z∪(8Z-p), v>=3, with a divisor d≡-1 mod v of p+v) for all 108,283 primes p≡1 (4), p<=3e6, v<=160: records 3(5),4(17),7(97),8(457),23(1009),87(2521),116(3361) exactly as the repo records. record.summary: Type I divisor condition (f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p mod 4cd) for 211 primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 3000, c ≤ 20, d ≤ 30: no solution ever occurs with d = 1 (0 of 211), and some solution exists for every prime with d ≤ 30 (smallest d: 2 in 110 cases, 3 in 34, 5 in 32, 6 in 10). Proof sketch: every prime divisor of p²+4c² is ≡ 1 (mod 4) (or equals p), so every divisor f ≡ 1 (mod 4), while f ≡ −p ≡ 3 (mod 4) is required; so Q(√−1) is excluded by a genus character. The residue condition is therefore a genus condition in Q(√−d), as the item suspected, and d = 1 is obstructed for all p ≡ 1 (mod 4).
record.not_done: The general-d genus criterion (which d are allowed for each p) not derived in full; the proof sketch covers d = 1 only.

title: Binary quadratic forms: Type I as representation of p² by a form of discriminant −16c²d
connection: f | p² + 4c²d means p² + 4c²d = f·g; representation theory of binary quadratic forms (Gauss composition) describes which f occur as 'first coefficients' of forms representing p² + 4c²d... Equivalently, (p, c·2√(−d)) is a vector in an imaginary quadratic order; the norm factorisation is governed by the class group of ℚ(√−d).

avenue.role: Type I as an ideal-divisor / ray-class condition in ℚ(√−d): 𝔞 | (p + 2c√−d) with N𝔞 ≡ −p (mod 4cd)
avenue.missing_theorem: For every prime p there are c, d and an ideal 𝔞 | (p + 2c√−d) whose ray class mod 4cd has norm ≡ −p. Chebotarev distributes prime ideals over ray classes on average; here 𝔞 must divide one specific element and the field and conductor move with (c, d) — the B2 event. The genus/BM part forces (d/p) = −1 (see Z1483).

record.summary: Round 3 with exact R(p) (ordered divisor pairs of 4p+1 with both factors = 3 mod 4), N<10^4 gives 2067 primes p=n^2+n+41 with p=1 mod 4 (max p ~ 10^8). For 4-chains (a,b,c,d) with continuant p ≡ 1 (8), p ≤ 3000, and cofactor A = K(b,c,d), the sign (A/p) is also a function of (a,b,c,d) mod 4 (6250 chains, 90 residue classes, 0 conflicts), while the naive rules ('4 | entry' or '4 | sub-continuant') match only 1348/1730 and 1216/1730 chains. title: Slot lemma as a van der Blij / Gauss–Milgram formula for odd lattices (characteristic covectors)
connection: For an odd lattice, the Gauss sum of the discriminant form is governed by σ − w² mod 8, where w is a characteristic covector (van der Blij, Brown invariant). For the chain lattice, w has coordinates (v,t,u) mod 2 and w² has denominator p. This plausibly yields (A/p) as a function of p mod 8 and the parity pattern of (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1), i.e. the slot lemma.

avenue.role: sign layer of the five-slice route ES₅ (and of the length-L ladder λ(p) ≤ L): a structural formula for the certificate bit (A/p) of a given word
avenue.missing_theorem: (a) Side theorem: for the odd chain lattice of an HJ word [a₁,…,a_L] with det p, (A/p) = F(σ − w² mod 8, p mod 8), w a characteristic covector — giving the correct sign rule for every L (the naive 'some diagonal ≡ 0 (4)' rule is false at L = 4, [2,2,2,5]). (b) ES step that would still be needed: for every prime p ≡ 1 (24) there is a positive word of length ≤ L with tuv − u − v = p (L = 3) whose van der Blij invariant takes the certificate value — which is ES₅ itself.

avenue.status_ref: slot lemma PROVED: FOREST_CONNECTIVITY.md Thm 2.1 (elementary, all edges), DEDEKIND_ES.md Thm 4.5; L ≥ 4 naive rule false (BRAINSTORM/z52b_translate.md item 270). The existence of a word with the right bit is ES₅ (FRONTIER §2.4, §7.14).

avenue.new_ingredient: none (a new proof of a known equivalence; L ≥ 4 sign rule is new bookkeeping, not a mechanism)

title: Class number one in the genus: search for an ES-encoding lattice with a one-class genus
connection: Gauss's three squares: local solvability + one class in the genus of x²+y²+z² ⇒ global. ES is locally solvable everywhere (Bright–Loughran); if ES(p) ⟺ a lattice L represents an invariant of p, and gen(L) has one class (or one spinor genus), ES follows.

avenue.role: local-global via a one-class genus (Gauss three-squares template)
avenue.missing_theorem: There is a lattice L whose genus has one class (or one spinor genus) such that ES(p) ⟺ L represents an invariant ι(p). For Type I/II solutions this is false: one-class genus ⇒ representability is local, and the Type I/II local, genus and spinor conditions all hold at odd squares m² where f_I = f_II = 0 (T1). So ι(m²) would be represented, giving a Type I/II solution at m². No fixed modulus separates squares from Mordell-hard primes, since square classes contain primes.
avenue.status_ref: FRONTIER §1 T1 and §6 'Local + spinor ⇒ global … true at odd squares' ((I)1, (I)4); CONDITIONAL_ES.md §7.4 (local hypotheses cannot imply X_slice); POINTWISE_TERNARY Cor 4.2

title: Check whether Type II with c ≥ 2 is itself just the C-form for a *composite* n: ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) ⟺ C-form certificate for n = cp with C = cd?
connection: C-form for n' = cp with C' = cd: 4C'n' + 1 = 4cd·cp + 1 = 4c²dp + 1 ✓ and a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C' = 4cd ✓. So Type II for p with parameters (c, d) is EXACTLY the C-form for the multiple n = cp with parameter C = cd. Hence: ES(p) via Type II ⟺ some multiple cp of p has a C-form certificate; and a solution for cp gives one for p by scaling?? NO — scaling goes the other way (solution for n gives one for multiples). Hmm: C-form for cp gives 4/(cp) = 1/(C'uv) + 1/(cpC'v) + 1/(cpC'u) ⟹ multiply by c: 4/p = c/(C'uv) + 1/(pC'v) + 1/(pC'u) — first term c/(cd·uv) = 1/(duv) ✓ a unit fraction! So yes: a C-form certificate for cp with C' = cd yields 4/p = 1/(duv) + 1/(pcdv) + 1/(pcdu). Consistent. So full Type II ⟺ 'some multiple cp of p, with C a multiple of c, has a C-form certificate' — the slack is exactly 'pass to a multiple'.

avenue.role: dictionary: Type II with parameters (c, d) ⟺ (★)/C-form certificate for the multiple n = cp with C = cd
avenue.missing_theorem: (Dictionary, PROVED here, elementary.) ff′ = 4c²dp + 1, f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) ⟺ a C-form certificate for n′ = cp at C′ = cd, and dividing by c returns 4/p = 1/(duv) + 1/(pcdv) + 1/(pcdu). So ES-Type-II(p) ⟺ ∃c ≥ 1: R_c(cp) ≥ 1 with c | C. The architecture 'prove (★) for some multiple' needs: for every prime p there is c with a C-form certificate of cp at C ∈ cℕ — which is ES-Type-II itself.

title: Type I in the shifted form: f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) — is there an analogous 'p + u has a divisor in a class' statement for Type I (c = 1: f | p² + 4d, f ≡ −p mod 4d)?
connection: By analogy with the C-form reparametrisation, Type I c = 1 should be expressible as 'some pu + 1 (or p·u + something) has a divisor in a class'. From the e-slice form: Type I ↔ N = (pe + 1)/4 — multiplicative shift pe + 1; Type II ↔ N = (p + e)/4 — additive shift. So the two types are 'additive shifts p + e' and 'multiplicative shifts pe + 1' of p, each needing a divisor in a tied class. The C-form (p + u with divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u) is the additive one; Type I c=1 should be: pe + 1 has a divisor ≡ (something) mod 4e... Derive precisely.

avenue.role: reformulation (organising principle): Type II c = 1 = additive shifts p + u, Type I c = 1 = multiplicative shifts pk + 1, each needing one divisor in a tied class
avenue.missing_theorem: Derived here (PROVED, elementary): Type I with c = 1 (f | p² + 4d, f ≡ −p (mod 4d)) ⟺ ∃ k ≥ 1 and g | pk + 1 with g ≡ −p (mod 4k), g > 0. [f = 4dk − p; gcd(f, 4d) = 1 gives f | 4dk² + 1 = k·f + (pk + 1).] Symmetric to (★): ∃ u, a | p + u, a ≡ −1 (mod 4u). The ES-relevant statement is then 'for every p one of the two shift families fires' — a union of two tied-class lower tails.

title: Per-level explicit thresholds: R_t(n) is exactly a divisor count — make each level's failure set explicit
connection: 290 theorem: explicit per-form cusp bounds + finite checks. ES levels have no cusp part (METAPLECTIC Thm K: R_t = D_t^− − β_t), so each level's failure set is an explicit multiplicative condition on tn+1. Compose them escalator-style.

avenue.role: finitely many levels + finite check (Bhargava escalator analogue): ES at every p from the union of explicit level failure sets S_t = {n : D_t⁻(tn+1) = β_t(n)}
avenue.missing_theorem: (Fixed-menu form) ∃ T: ∩_{4|t≤T} S_t contains only finitely many primes. CONDITIONAL-FALSE: under Hypothesis H every fixed finite menu of slices fails for infinitely many p ≡ 1 (24) (B2(iii)); unconditionally this is open only because exhibiting such primes needs tp+1 to have restricted factorisation for all t ≤ T at once (a Schinzel/H-type input); odd squares lie in every S_t (T1). (Growing form, open) every prime p > p₀ has a level 4C ≤ (log p)^A such that 4Cp+1 has a divisor d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) with 4C − 1 < d < (4Cp+1)/(4C − 1) (a non-boundary (★) word; a one-coordinate polylog window on the level).

title: Index argument: subgroup generated by prime factors of N in (ℤ/4C)*
connection: Artin-type proofs control the index of ⟨a⟩ in F_p*. ES level C fails iff no subproduct of prime factors of N = 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 (4C). If the factors generate a subgroup H ∌ −1, failure is automatic; if −1 ∈ H, failure needs few factors. Study the index of H as p varies.

avenue.role: split the tied divisor event at a level C into an algebraic part (−1 ∈ H_C := ⟨prime factors of N_C = 4Cp+1⟩ ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^×) and a combinatorial part (−1 is a 0/1-exponent subproduct)
avenue.missing_theorem: For every large prime p some C has −1 ∈ H_C AND −1 is a subproduct ∏_{q|N_C} q^{a_q} with 0 ≤ a_q ≤ v_q(N_C) (mod 4C). The first half alone is the exponent-cap relaxation (provable-type, CAP_POINTWISE (J)64); the second half is cap 0, i.e. the tied divisor event itself.
avenue.yield: ES (both halves); the first half alone yields only a cap relaxation
avenue.status_ref: Second half = B2 at level C (FRONTIER §2.1 divisor form); first half = 'self-generated mute set' mechanism ((J)64, FRONTIER §5.2: reciprocity forces −1 ∈ ⟨primes of x⟩, cap 0 is the B2 event). Cheap check (this pass, scripts/z52d_avenue_P02_index.py, C ≤ 150, EVIDENCE): at all 14 (★)-zeros, −1 ∈ H_C at 480/2100 levels (23 %) with no hit; at 14 matched controls −1 ∈ H_C at 584/2100 (28 %) of which 84 hit (14 %). So zeros are not 'algebraic' failures: −1 is generated at ~34 levels per zero prime; failure is combinatorial (exponent caps).
avenue.barrier: B2 (the combinatorial half), cap-0 gap (B-fin: Q | (r+1)/4 vs rad(Q) | (r+1)/4)

title: Potential ES: count solutions over a quadratic field and use Galois parity
connection: Potential automorphy proves things over extensions and descends via Brauer induction. ES over O_K for real quadratic K: Gal(K/ℚ) acts on K-solutions of 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z with totally positive x,y,z; fixed points are ℚ-solutions. If the number of K-solutions in a Galois-stable finite window is odd, a rational solution exists.

avenue.role: descent by Galois parity: potential ES over a real quadratic K
avenue.missing_theorem: For some real quadratic K and every p, the number of totally positive O_K-solutions of 4/p = Σ1/x_i in a Gal(K/ℚ)-stable finite set is odd. Non-rational solutions pair under conjugation, so the K-count ≡ the ℚ-count (mod 2). The missing theorem is therefore the same as 'the ℚ-count in that set is odd', which is ES itself in parity form. Any count-parity theorem must also see the quadratic character, since the Type I/II count is 0 at odd squares (M5 row).
avenue.status_ref: FRONTIER §3 M-pattern table row M5 (count congruences must see the quadratic character; finite-menu affine involutions barred, (J)2 CONDITIONAL); BRAINSTORM/other_rings.md
avenue.next: Close. The K-side adds no independent handle on parity.

record.summary: Read the abstract of Tseng (Math. Z. 302 (2022), arXiv:2106.00836, verified via arXiv API): a closed horocycle of length ℓ equidistributes on the cusp neighbourhood shrinking at rate T^{−1} whenever T/ℓ→0 (segment condition max{T^{−1/6},(T/ℓ)^{1/2}}(T/ℓ)^{−δ}, which is trivial for the full closed horocycle). So the deepest reachable target for a closed horocycle of length p has measure ≈1/T with T=p^{1−o(1)}, i.e. measure p^{−1+o(1)}, and the expected number of visits is ℓ/T=p^{o(1)}. Kelmer (arXiv:1708.08953) treats logarithm laws/shrinking targets for discrete flows and does not give the closed-horocycle depth.
record.not_done: Matching the ES target's normalisation (horocycle length and cusp height convention) to Tseng's T; the statement is about one horocycle of length ℓ, the ES family is p orbits.
record.next: Check bsA's target normalisation against Tseng's T and length ℓ; if they match, the ES-target depth p^{−1+ε} is inside Tseng's range.

title: Shrinking-target property for every closed horocycle
connection: Logarithm laws (Kleinbock–Margulis) give deep excursions for almost every orbit; ES would need them for the specific closed horocycle of length p and depth ~ p^{θ}. Tseng (Math. Z. 2022) proves shrinking-cusp-target equidistribution for long closed horocycles (effective version included).

avenue.role: deep cusp excursions of the closed horocycle of length p force a QNR length-3 HJ expansion
avenue.missing_theorem: For every prime p, the points {(A + i)/p : (A/p) = −1} of the closed horocycle meet the union of length-3 HJ cylinders (total measure ≍ log²p/p). Shrinking-target equidistribution (Tseng, Kelmer) works for targets of measure ≥ p^{−θ}, θ < 1. A target of measure p^{−1+o(1)} with polylog expected hits is the single-integer lower tail.
avenue.yield: ES (via ES₅); relaxations only for power-size targets
avenue.status_ref: FRONTIER §3 B3; BRAINSTORM/bsA_hecke_cusp_excursions.md
avenue.next: Close. Reading Tseng would only confirm θ < 1.
avenue.note: A deep excursion gives a large partial quotient, not a short HJ length; both are 'cusp' events, but ES₅ needs ≤ 3 HJ steps.

title: Positivity from an exact divisor-sum formula: where the tail can be bounded
connection: For the partition function, positivity is trivial but Lehmer bounded the Rademacher tail explicitly. ES level counts are exact divisor-class sums (R_t(n) = D_t^−(tn+1) − β_t(n)); summing over t with weights, the 'tail' is the order-≥3 character part X(n). Ask for the explicit size of X(n) relative to M_BM in the exact formula at small levels.

avenue.role: explicit tail bound in the exact formula: X(p)/M_BM(p) stays above −1
avenue.missing_theorem: X(p) ≥ −(1 − ε)M_gen(p) (equivalently R(p) ≥ ε·M_gen(p)) for every large prime p.
avenue.status_ref: This is H⁻_BM in genus form (FRONTIER §2.4: 'ES-(★) in disguise up to ε'); the two-sided version |X| < M_gen is false i.o. (Prop 3.1). Lehmer's Rademacher-tail bound works because the tail is an absolutely convergent explicit series; X(p) is a sum of ≍ p log p order-≥ 3 character terms with no decay.
avenue.next: None. (Plot X/M_BM for p ≤ 10⁷ if data is wanted; at the 14 (★)-failures it is −M_gen/M_BM by definition.)
avenue.note: The exact formula is known (genus split, Thm K); the tail is the problem.

Intermediate ES goal: prove ES (or (★)) for all p in the set {p : (p/ℓ) = −1} for one fixed ℓ (e.g. ℓ = 3 excluded by Mordell classes; ℓ = 11, 13, …), where the BM main term at levels involving ℓ is guaranteed.

title: Variance-to-mean ratio of R(p) as a quasi-independence diagnostic
connection: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard's key was showing overlaps are small on average (quasi-independence). For ES, the variance of R(p) over primes near X relative to its mean measures overlap; Poisson-like behaviour (ratio ≈ 1 after removing the genus fluctuation) indicates quasi-independent events.
